sentences.text: Devincenzia was a more robust terror bird adapted for ambush hunting compared to its relatives Phorusrhacos and Titanis.
The preserved skull measured approximately 64.5 centimeters in length, though it was flattened by taphonomic processes and required extensive plaster reconstruction.
Anatomical features of the foot bone show a mix of traits found in agile phorusrhacines and heavy brontornithines.
The largest possible specimen may have stood 2 meters tall and weighed between 200 and 500 kilograms.
This species was uniquely adapted for ambush hunting rather than the pursuit strategies seen in other large birds.
Large expansions on the eye socket likely protected the eyes from the sun, indicating keen vision in open, sunlit areas.
The genus Devincenzia was formally named by Kraglievich in 1932.
Initial fossils attributed to the group were unearthed in 1933 near Lake Epecuén in Buenos Aires Province.
These early remains were cataloged at the MACN with the numbers MACN PV 6554 and MACN PV 6681.
Fossils of Onactornis depressus, considered a possible synonym, were found in the Cerro Azul Formation dating between 10 and 5.7 million years ago.
Currently, there are 4 recorded fossil occurrences of Devincenzia in the Paleobiology Database.
This animal was carnivorous and possibly acted as a scavenger.
Alvarenga and Höfling suggested phorusrhacids were flightless based on wing-to-body mass proportions, noting that wing size was more reduced in larger members.
Researchers suggested future studies should examine if phorusrhacids used beaks and claws against well-armored mammals like armadillos and glyptodonts.
Researchers assumed the neck adaptations found in Andalgalornis would also apply to other large phorusrhacids like Devincenzia.
Studies suggest that while both skull types handled prey similarly, the rigid skulls of the Terror Bird type were an adaptation for handling larger prey.
Kraglievich originally placed Devincenzia in its own family, Devincenziidae, within Stereornithes.
Recent studies consider Psilopteridae and Devincenziidae synonymous with Phorusrhacidae, but Opisthodactylidae and Brontornithidae contain genera not included in Phorusrhacidae.
Devincenzia belongs to the family Phorusrhacidae.
The time range for Devincenzia is estimated from 29 to 5 million years ago.
The Ituzaingó Formation dates to the Late Miocene, a time of high biodiversity in South America.
Phorusrhacids dispersed into North America during the Great American Biotic Interchange approximately 3 million years ago.
Whether Onactornis and Devincenzia are synonyms remains a subject of debate.
The discovery of Kelenken challenged the traditional view that larger phorusrhacids were less agile and adapted for running.
Assignments of remains from Africa, Europe, and the Paleocene of Brazil to Phorusrhacidae or as related to seriemas remain controversial.
Agnolín's stance on Phorusrhacinae composition was backed by a phylogenetic analysis finding Kelenken and Devincenzia as sister taxa.
